newsitem.title: FRANCE: Algera's industry output falls, energy rises.
newsitem.headline: Algera's industry output falls, energy rises.

text.p: Algeria's industrial output fell 6.2 percent in the first nine months of 1996 compared with the same period in 1995, official figures showed on Tuesday.

But oil and gas output, the mainstay of the North African country's economy, rose by 5.7 percent, according to National Official of Statistics (ONS) data carried by the government-controlled newspaper El Moudjahid. Electricity output grew 3.9 percent.
The iron and steel industry was the worst hit in the first nine months of 1996, when output sank 18.7 percent. Chemical industry output fell 17.1 percent.
The data did not mention the impact of the civil strife on output but the ONS said "industrial activity continues to be affected by cash flow and imported raw material problems".
Building materials output was an exception, rising to satisfy the state's plan to build about 160,000 homes to ease Algeria's crippling housing shortage of more than one million units.
ONS said building materials production jumped by 4.2 percent, including a 11.6 percent rise in cement output.
Early in 1996 the government ordered state-owned cement firms to raise production above their then-current 60 percent of capacity to slash costly cement imports.

Algeria's cement plants have a combined capacity of 11.6 million of tonnes but are producing far below that level because of technical and managerial problems. Algeria imports an estimated 2.0 million tonnes per year.
An official report early in 1996 said that sabotage by Moslem guerrillas trying to topple President Liamine Zeroual's government had crippled 10 percent of non-oil-and-gas industrial activity.
Official estimates said sabotage had caused more than $2.0 billion in losses for the overall economy.
About 60,000 people have been killed in Algeria's violence since early 1992 when the authorities cancelled a general election in which radical Islamists had taken a huge lead.
